newsitem.title: UK: Child abuse film causes uproar in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Child abuse film causes uproar in Britain.

text.p: A television drama about sexual abuse of children caused uproar in Britain on Wednesday and debate whether the events it portrayed were fact or fiction.

Two years in the making, "No Child of Mine" is the supposedly true-life story of Kerry, who told the programme-makers she endured sexual torment as a child at the hands of her mother, stepfather and a care worker and was forced into prostitution by her father.

Even before the 90-minute film was broadcast in Britain late on Tuesday -- with a warning that viewers might find it harrowing -- it provoked outrage that an actress aged only 13, Brooke Kinsella, had taken part in the simulation of acts of sexual abuse.
Some child care experts warned that the program might encourage paedophiles while social service workers said efforts to check Kerry's story had cast doubts on her accusations.

"I am not prepared to conclude that the abuse she says she suffered as a child did not take place, but this woman has a proven track record as a liar," the director of social services told the Guardian newspaper.
The Department of Health, which reportedly knows Kerry's real identity, issued a statement saying it had no evidence that events shown in the film actually happened.

But Peter Kosminsky, a seasoned documentary director, defended his film, saying Kerry's story had been thoroughly checked. Meridian, the broadcasting company that commissioned it, also gave full backing.
"The research includes corroboration from care workers, counsellors and social workers," the company said.

Before beginning the project Kosminsky said he had consulted Childline, a helpline for abused children, about the subjects he should look into. The group suggest conveyor belt abuse, where the child is abuse at home, then in care and later lured into prostitution.

"A child who has had a lousy start should be put in a place of safety. Instead, our society puts them in places of danger where they are exposed to further abuse. That compounds the negligence and pain," he said in an interview.

Kerry, now an adult who reportedly works in social services where she was in care, has admitted making up some allegations claiming that she was suffering from "flashbacks" of the real abuse she had suffered.
Children welfare agencies were divided about the film.
The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children told the Guardian, "We know this is one child's true experience of sexual exploitation."
Others groups weren't so sure and claimed that if some of the facts in the film were false it could harm the work of social workers.

As the controversy swirled around "No Child of Mine", a special tribunal, ordered by Prime Minister John Major last year, was investigating complaints by 180 former residents of children's' homes in North Wales who claimed they had been abused by 85 employees at the residences.
The tribunal is expected to last a year and cost up to 10 million pounds ($16.4 million).
